overview: Dutch Brazil was a West India Company colony in northeastern Brazil, established by conquest in 1630 and lost in 1654. Sugar production, slavery, religious communities and ambitious scientific collecting shaped its short history. The imported map’s 1650 to 1715 range must not be mistaken for the colony’s actual lifespan.

periods.title: Conquest and occupation
periods.summary: The company seized Portuguese territory and its established sugar economy.

periods.title: Johan Maurits in Brazil
periods.summary: The governor supported mills, art and scientific investigation within a society dependent on slavery.

periods.title: Final decade of Dutch government
periods.summary: Dutch rule ended with surrender and Portuguese recovery in January 1654.

items.text: Johan Maurits provided loans for Portuguese operators to reopen abandoned sugar mills. Dutch officials depended on people already familiar with the industry. Taking control of a colony did not instantly supply the practical knowledge needed to run its machinery and plantations.

Plantation labor was coerced. Enslaved African men, women and children were transported to Dutch Brazil, and the governor personally owned and traded enslaved people. His support for painting and science cannot be separated from the violence that supported colonial wealth.

Drawings associated with Zacharias Wagener record a Recife slave market and a woman branded with Johan Maurits’s initials. These are rare visual witnesses to an experience that polished colonial landscapes often concealed. They depict real systems of ownership and dehumanization.

Two religious schools, Talmud Torah and Etz Hayim, operated beside the Kahal Zur Israel synagogue. Rabbi Isaac Aboab da Fonseca arrived in Recife in 1642 at the community’s invitation. Worship, study and migration linked this neighborhood to Jewish communities across the Atlantic.

Excavation at the synagogue site revealed eight floor levels, fragments of Dutch pipes, glazed pottery and a ceramic piece with a menorah. These finds show how a building accumulated changes and everyday objects. The furniture now displayed there was reconstructed through research, not found intact.

The site also preserves a mikveh, a bath for religious purification. This gives a concrete glimpse of ritual life involving water. It should not be treated as evidence that every Recife household had the same bathing arrangements.

Frans Post’s Brazilian Landscape with a House under Construction presents European, Indigenous and African figures in an apparently harmonious setting. The museum cautions that this idealized scene hides slavery’s harsh realities. A painting can preserve useful details while also giving a misleading impression of society.

Post made the painting after returning to the Netherlands. His Brazilian scenes therefore combine remembered experience with later artistic choices. They are valuable historical evidence, but not snapshots taken while the events unfolded.

Collectors did not work alone: Indigenous Brazilians, enslaved Africans and Portuguese residents brought specimens to naturalists. Research tracing the surviving botanical images emphasizes these often uncredited contributions. The knowledge printed under European authors’ names depended on many other people.

A surviving plant specimen, an oil painting and a printed woodcut can be compared for Spigelia anthelmia, recorded as a remedy for intestinal worms. That chain shows how plant knowledge entered books. It documents historical medicine, not a recommendation to use the plant today.

The same research follows Cleome gynandra, an African leafy vegetable eaten by enslaved Africans in Brazil. Editor Johannes de Laet grew seeds in the Netherlands in 1646, but the plant died as the weather turned cold. Food plants traveled with people, even across climates where they struggled.

“Historia naturalis Brasiliae” means “Natural history of Brazil.” This Latin title appears on the 1648 book preserved in the John Carter Brown Library. It is an authentic printed sample of scholarly writing connected with the colony, rather than a reconstruction of ordinary conversation.

ending.text: Dutch forces surrendered in January 1654, returning the occupied region to Portuguese rule. This ended the colonial government, not the lives or histories of its diverse inhabitants. The imported 1715 endpoint is incorrect for Dutch Brazil and remains a map-data issue to correct.
